analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from making workers sign non-compete agreements.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made non-compete agreements unenforceable nationwide, was introduced in April 2018, referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have outlawed agreements that stop an employee from going to work for a competing company, taking a job in a certain area, or doing similar work after leaving. Such agreements would automatically be treated as illegal restraints of competition unless the employer proved otherwise. Workers who were made to sign one could sue for damages and attorney's fees, while employers could still protect genuine trade secrets.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers bound by non-compete agreements, who gain the freedom to change jobs, bargain for higher pay, or start their own businesses without fear of being sued. Non-competes reach far beyond executives: they are common for low-wage and mid-wage workers in fast food, staffing, health care, and other service sectors.

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits any employer covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act from entering a covenant not to compete with an employee.
A non-compete in an employment contract is presumed illegal as anticompetitive unless the employer proves by a preponderance of the evidence that its pro-competitive effects outweigh the harm.
Workers can sue in federal court for actual damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees and costs if they win.
It preserves employers' ability to stop employees from disclosing trade secrets, addressing the most legitimate employer concern.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use non-compete agreements to keep workers from leaving for competitors, or to hold down wages by limiting workers' outside options, lose that tool. Some firms that pay for training argue they would lose more employees to competitors, although the bill leaves trade-secret protections intact.

drawbacks.text: Employers legitimately argue that non-competes protect their investment in training and confidential business relationships, and a blanket ban removes that option even in cases where those interests are real.

The bill creates a private right of action with punitive damages and attorney's fees, which could generate litigation costs for employers over agreements signed in good faith, even though trade secrets are carved out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most workers the benefits are substantial: research on states that have restricted non-competes shows workers move more freely and earn more when they can switch employers. The costs fall on firms that relied on non-competes to retain trained staff, and litigation risk is a real but manageable objection, particularly since the bill preserves trade-secret agreements. On balance the worker gains outweigh the employer losses, and the bill was a clean, enforceable design rather than a half-measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary and Education and Workforce committees and then to a Judiciary subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Crowley introduced the bill on April 26, 2018, joined by original cosponsors including Reps. Sanchez, Pocan, Ellison, Nadler, and Cicilline.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Education and the Workforce Committee, the standard first step that does not require a vote.
On May 22, 2018, the Judiciary Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
No further action of any kind appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use non-compete agreements to limit where their workers can work and how much they can bargain kept that tool unchanged. Workers bound by non-competes gained nothing from this Congress.

industries.industry: Employers using non-compete agreements (fast food and service franchises, staffing agencies, health systems, tech firms)
industries.note: The bill would strip employers of a contract that limits workers' ability to change jobs, which employers use to reduce turnover and hold down outside offers. Workers' gain from mobility is exactly what these firms would give up.

Franchisors often use non-competes to keep franchisees and managers from moving to rival brands; the ban would disrupt that practice while leaving ordinary franchise workers free to move, a genuine two-sided effect but not a large one for the sector overall.
